original_numbered_lines.text: Autoformalization requires both faithful interpretation and a computational route
for reasoning about it. We describe a compiler-guided architecture coupling en-
gineered symbolic IRs to adaptive multi-view representation learning. Determin-
istic parsers construct source-grounded declarations; decompilers expose source-
withheld reconstruction errors; and shared feature, family, semantic-slot, and view
parameters are optimized by an implemented packed tensor update and guarded
outer selection. BM25, vector indexes, and knowledge-graph traversal supply
complementary context rather than truth criteria. A policy-constrained Tactician
organizes search, an ITP Hammer translates supported fragments and reconstructs
solver candidates, and Leanstral supplies advisory proof-engineering proposals. In-
dependently admitted feedback trains isolated proof heads or motivates separately
tested compiler/decompiler changes. Stable learned guidance reaches enabled
consumers only through source-free, fixed-canary promotion. Shared symbols
and explicit preservation contracts connect deontic, temporal, frame, event, graph,
Legal, Security, and Intent views without equating their semantics. We distinguish
numerical reconstruction from symbolic round trips, and model prediction from
checked proof. A synthetic policy–code–trace example and twelve standalone
semantic checks illustrate composition. This source-audited methods draft reports
no new checkpoint training or end-to-end performance: held-out source fidelity,
retrieval benefit, native proof coverage, and total learning/verification cost remain
to be measured.
1    Introduction
Autoformalization makes heterogeneous material available to mechanical reasoning, but a formula
can be well typed and provable while misrepresenting its source. A requirement, implementation, and
execution trace also have different truth conditions: an obligation is not an observation, permission
is not execution, and belief is not fact. Recent mathematical autoformalization demonstrates useful
natural-language translation into formal statements [1, 2, 9]. Our question is how to learn better
source-to-symbolic mappings while preserving these distinctions across domains and logical views.
The method couples a deterministic semantic pipeline to adaptive representation learning. Compilers
create source-grounded intermediate representations (IRs), decomposers expose multiple logical
views, and decompilers reconstruct inspectable content. An adaptive modal autoencoder learns
reusable feature-to-embedding and feature-to-family/view parameters against these targets. Recon-
struction, structural, provenance, grammar, and cross-view diagnostics identify where the symbolic
pipeline is inadequate. Bounded optimization then either updates model parameters or proposes a
separately validated compiler/decompiler improvement. Checked proof feedback supplies additional,
isolated prediction heads rather than rewarding arbitrary changes that make the input easier to prove.
This is neither one end-to-end language model nor an unsupervised discovery of a universal logic.
The schema, operators, sorts, and admissibility rules are engineered. Learning estimates content,
associations, rankings, and repair priorities within those contracts. Several paths coexist: determin-
istic compilation, adaptive diagnostic learning, genuine tensor gradient updates, source-withheld
reconstruction, and bounded model-assisted synthesis. We distinguish their inputs, outputs, objectives,
and activation instead of describing all of them as one autoencoder.
The contribution of this methods draft is: (i) a source-grounded account of representation learn-
ing and compiler/decompiler improvement; (ii) an explicit account of BM25, vector, and graph
retrieval, policy-constrained proof planning, Hammer reconstruction, and Leanstral guidance; and
(iii) composition of complementary IR views through typed identities and justified translations. A
worked policy–code–trace example and finite semantic witnesses illustrate the necessary boundaries.
The final learned-fidelity, transfer, checkpoint, and cost experiments remain marked for completion.
Source inspection establishes implementation mechanisms, not successful training of every optional
configuration.
2     Representations and training examples
2.1   What is shared, and what is learned?
Three axes must remain distinct. Source format names prose, code, traces, tables, or extracted media.
Domain names Legal, Security, Intent, software, or UI declarations. Logical view names deontic,
temporal, frame, first-order, cognitive/event, graph, or proof-oriented structure. Sharing canonical
records does not equate domain ontologies or logical interpretations. [artifact S01–S06]
The domain-neutral kernel supplies canonical bytes, identities, provenance, source spans, assumptions,
claims, obligations, and result protocols. Domain adapters retain their own semantic slots. The syntax
kernel supplies typed terms, binders, signatures, connectives, and versioned family extensions. A
symbolic declaration is therefore discrete and inspectable; its CID identifies an encoding under a
declared profile, not a learned location in a vector space. Equal vectors or nearby embeddings do not
imply equivalent formulas. [artifact S01,S05]
Six intermediate objects have different roles: canonical symbolic declarations, family-specific
formulas, learned numerical features, graph relationships, search plans, and proof/evidence records.
A search plan is not a formula; a declaration is not its verification result; and a vector is not a proof.
Their interchange requires explicit mappings. A model can select or repair a candidate without
defining its semantics. [artifact S01,S04,S34,S38]
2.2   How examples and supervisory targets are constructed
The concrete legal training record contains source identity and citation, raw and normalized text,
an embedding-model identifier and vector, a modal IR document, frame candidates and selection,
parser trace, and losses. A builder normalizes a U.S.-Code-style passage, parses modal formulas,
ranks ontology frames using BM25, and packages the result. The default convenience embedding is
explicitly a deterministic mock; the local codec can instead supply spaCy-derived feature hashing,
and externally supplied vectors carry their producer identity. Experiments must record which path
supplied the target vector. [artifact S22,S23]
Thus targets are not all human gold labels. Modal-family targets can be derived from parsed operators;
view targets come from bridge contracts and their configured scoring; frames can be retrieval-selected;
and proof-feedback labels require admitted verifier records. Reproducing these labels measures
distillation of those teachers. Independent annotations and held-out semantic distinctions are required
to measure fidelity to the original source.
For a source x, write I = Cψ (x) for the symbolic compiler output, e = T (x) for the declared embed-
ding target, and f = F (x, I) for reusable features. Features include lexical cues, actor/action/object
roles, conditions and exceptions, temporal structure, predicate arity, quantifier scope, provenance,
frame relations, compiler contracts, and reconstruction diagnostics. The adaptive model predicts an
embedding ê, a modal-family distribution pF , and a view distribution pV . Some features depend on
an existing parse, so this is often parser-assisted learning, not a demonstrated raw-text-only universal
compiler. [artifact S24]
3     Compilers, decompilers, and reconstruction loops
3.1   The deterministic source-to-symbolic path
The local modal codec uses deterministic registry cues, spaCy-derived features, BM25 frame ground-
ing, and frame-logic consistency checks. It produces a structured modal declaration before optional
expensive model repair. A separate selected structured-text profile has a narrower seven-field rule:
modality, actor, action, object, conditions, exceptions, and temporal qualifiers. Its modality vo-
cabulary is obligation, permission, and prohibition; its atom vocabulary is supplied by the caller.
Unsupported semantics trigger abstention or disclosed partial output. The selected profile explicitly
disables learned guidance and repair: training elsewhere in the repository does not imply that this
frozen profile silently uses it. [artifact S07,S08,S23,S25]
Formalization adapters produce named formula views and source maps. The maps bind IR constituents
to source evidence; they are not proof of a correct interpretation. Source-code extraction offers
additional candidate security facts, with explicit heuristic and coverage limitations. Media requires a
separately measured extraction layer before this logic pipeline; no end-to-end audio/image theorem
performance is established here. [artifact S09,S13–S16]
3.2   Two different meanings of reconstruction
Symbolic reconstruction follows
A decompiler renders roles, predicates, modality, conditions, exceptions, and temporal structure
into inspectable text. The canonical source-withheld evaluation gives the realizer the IR, not the
originating source, its locator, source map, private parser state, or gold target. Comparing I1 and I2
tests reconstructable facets and compiler/realizer consistency. It does not prove source fidelity: both
programs could consistently omit the same exception. [artifact S07]
The adaptive autoencoder’s numerical reconstruction is different. Its encode method builds a state
containing family predictions and an embedding projection; its decode returns that projection as
a numeric vector. Its basic reconstruction target is the sample embedding, not arbitrary source
prose. Textual decompilation and structural cycle metrics enter through the codec and multi-view
bridge. Calling this vector reconstruction a trained free-text decoder would misstate the inspected
implementation. [artifact S24]
3.3   Constrained candidates and transfer beyond the legal teacher
The constrained decoder gives learned heads a closed production space: valid-token, grammar, binder,
type, and family masks precede candidate scoring. The inspected profile declares a frozen 143-token
vocabulary and bounded search, but these declarations are not a learned tokenizer checkpoint or
evidence of end-to-end sequence training. The learner may rank admitted productions; a deterministic
grammar decides what can be represented. [artifact S33]
The original sample builder is legal-specific. A domain-neutral formalization/advisor layer permits
other domain adapters to share feature, view, checkpoint, and result contracts, but it does not
automatically turn a legal-trained model into a calibrated Security or Intent formalizer. Cross-domain
use needs explicit adapter mappings and separate evaluation. Shared infrastructure, statistical transfer,
and semantic proof transfer are three distinct claims. [artifact S01,S17,S22]
4     Adaptive multi-view learning
4.1   Shared parameter state versus per-example memory
The adaptive implementation has sparse parameter groups for feature embeddings, modal families,
semantic slots, predicate arguments, logic signatures, view logits, decompiler plans, and family–slot–
view interactions. It also retains compatibility fields indexed by sample identity. The generalizable
training route disables per-sample memory for updates and evaluation; accepted improvements must
come from shared feature parameters. This distinction is essential because reconstructing a stored
vector for a known sample is not generalization. [artifact S24]
A schematic description of the shared heads is
Here Ag is the activity of a bounded feature group, and Wg , Ug , Vg stand for enabled embedding and
logit tables. This notation summarizes the packed implementation, not a claim that it is a Transformer
or variational autoencoder. Some groups may be disabled, and a forward-only no-op is reported
separately from a parameter update. [artifact S26–S28]
4.2   Actual gradient objectives
The packed tensor implementation gathers active rows, constructs predictions, reduces losses in
FP32, backpropagates, clips gradients, applies an SGD-style step, and scatters changed rows into
transaction-aware state. BF16 activations are optional after a numerical check; the same packed
path has a CPU reference. This is real differentiation through tensor losses, not just the word “SGD”
applied to a prose critique loop. The inspected update is not an Adam update. [artifact S26–S28]
For the active heads, its objective is
Targets are normalized distributions; masks exclude unavailable target rows. Reconstruction is
averaged over embedding coordinates, cosine loss guards zero-norm vectors, the auxiliary term
penalizes extreme norm ratios, and regularization is normalized over parameters. Terms for inactive
update targets are zero. The outer controller additionally scores structural/view losses and regression
constraints; it is not simply Equation 5 applied to every available metric. [artifact S27]
Family targets may be mixed. Evaluation reports cross-entropy, target entropy, and excess cross-
entropy. Since H(q, p) − H(q) = DKL (q∥p), a nonzero cross-entropy need not be avoidable error:
it can include the target distribution’s own entropy. Neither cosine similarity nor cross-entropy is a
theorem about recovered meaning. [artifact S24]
4.3   Guarded optimization rather than an unrestricted fit
The generalizable projection trainer selects update groups—family logits, decoded embeddings,
global or feature-specific view logits, and combined updates—and evaluates candidate learning-rate
steps. It can concentrate on hard examples, use bounded pre-screening, and select a candidate only
when the chosen objective improves without disallowed regression. Candidate changes are evaluated
transactionally and rolled back before selection; timeout, no-improvement, and regression remain
visible. A configurable deadband can relax a named numerical tolerance, so its mode and protected
metrics belong in the experiment manifest. [artifact S24]
Validation examples supplied to this repeated selection procedure are model-selection data, not an
untouched test set. Moreover, when no validation set is supplied, the inspected function falls back
to evaluating training samples. The paper’s generalization claims therefore require explicit disjoint
source-family splits, separate final test data, disabled sample memory, and frozen targets. Source
derivatives and multiple views of one passage must not cross partitions.
4.4   Proof-aware auxiliary supervision
Seven explicit heads predict obligation family, semantic slots, premise family, route availability,
trusted outcome, reconstruction success, and minimal failing contract. Categorical heads use nor-
malized class probabilities; multilabel heads use independent sigmoid probabilities. Only version-
matched, trusted, eligible feedback trains them; duplicates and excluded holdout records are tracked.
The code reports coverage, abstention, and family-specific metrics. [artifact S24]
Critically, these proof-head parameters are isolated. Their declared weight in the primary representa-
tion objective is zero, and protected compiler cross-entropy, embedding, structural reconstruction,
provenance, and anti-copy parameter fingerprints are checked before and after an update. A prediction
of proof success can prioritize a route but cannot certify a formula. This protects against learning to
replace a difficult source statement with an easier, different theorem. [artifact S24]
4.5   How learning improves deterministic formalization
Introspection exposes feature contributions, embedding residuals, family margins, underrepresented
view components, and pipeline-stage diagnostics. The TODO supervisor separates parameter updates
from deterministic program-synthesis tasks. A high reconstruction loss can request a shared-weight
update; a missing exception-scoping rule requires a compiler/decompiler repair and new regression
tests. The cost-gated loop avoids expensive model repair unless it is enabled and its configured
expected benefit exceeds call cost. Those estimates are decisions to evaluate, not measured economic
guarantees. [artifact S24,S25,S29]
Stable-feature promotion is an explicit join between the two loops. The export excludes raw source,
token-level copying channels, sample identifiers, and sample-memory state. Integration resolves it
against canonical view contracts and requires paired, fixed-canary evidence, including source-copy
and symbolic-validity guardrails, before emitting content-addressed guidance with rollback metadata.
This is a guarded transfer of learned regularities into a deterministic compiler-facing interface, not
gradient descent through arbitrary parser code and not unconstrained rule invention. [artifact S30]
5     Retrieval, tacticians, and proof reconstruction
5.1   Three retrieval signals, not three truth criteria
BM25 supplies lexical candidates: the sample builder ranks frames, while a separate GraphRAG thin
client reads sharded postings and applies term-frequency, inverse-frequency, and length-normalization
scoring. Vector indexes instead retrieve neighbors of a declared embedding; the inspected FAISS
store maintains indexes, metadata, and identifier mappings. Graph adjacency and bounded walks
expand typed relationships and dependencies. These signals answer different questions—matching
terms, numerical similarity, and explicit connectivity—and none establishes entailment. [artifact
Index construction is not encoder training. Nor does a common result envelope establish that every
entry point supports every mode: the inspected thin-client CLI declares a vector option but does not
dispatch it to an implemented vector query. The actual producer, backend, revision, and route must
be recorded. Context found by any index becomes a premise only after grounding, applicability, and
policy checks; absence from retrieval is not logical negation. Appendix N details these boundaries.
5.2   The Tactician plans; the Hammer searches and reconstructs
The repository’s LogicTactician deterministically orders caller-provided sources under an explicit
policy, records selected/excluded routes, creates an acyclic subgoal plan, and reports stop or abstention
conditions. Planning performs no proof, network work, or writes. Optional model guidance can
reorder or nominate admitted sources under a pinned digest, with deterministic fallback. This planner
is not itself a trained tactic synthesizer. [artifact S38]
The ITP Hammer selects premises, lowers a supported first-order-safe fragment to TPTP or SMT-
LIB, runs an allowed bounded solver portfolio, and attempts native reconstruction. Vampire/E are
first-order automation routes; Z3/cvc5 are SMT routes; Lean, Coq/Rocq, and Isabelle/HOL have
separate frontend/reconstruction contracts. A logic family specifies what a statement means; a prover
family specifies a computation over an admitted encoding. Unsupported dependent, higher-order, or
unresolved polymorphic constructs cannot be silently erased. External execution is opt-in, and native
availability must be established. [artifact S37]
Within this Hammer contract, solver output is a candidate until reconstruction is accepted by the
originating ITP’s checker in its pinned environment. The deterministic premise baseline uses symbol,
type, import, and graph overlap, not a universal vector ranker. Its optional graph-selector artifact uses
hand-authored linear weights; the inspected release does not ship a genuinely trained premise-selector
checkpoint. Ranking machinery, training a ranker, and proving a goal are separate claims. [artifact
5.3   Leanstral proposals and verified training feedback
Leanstral supplies advisory proof-engineering candidates, such as Lean edits or strategies. The
security lane requires the suggested proof to pass the Lean checker and rejects proof bypasses; a
model response does not replace source, runtime, or release evidence. The legal rollout separately
admits structured guidance through syntax, provenance, anti-copy, proof, and configured Lean-
reconstruction checks. Raw drafts never become reconstruction targets or trusted training labels.
Verification creates a new structured artifact rather than making the original prose authoritative.
[artifact S39,S40]
Together, retrieval nominates context, the Tactician organizes bounded work, Hammer and Leanstral
provide different proposal mechanisms, and checking determines the supported result. Admitted feed-
back can train isolated heads or identify a compiler defect; a versioned patch still needs independent
regression tests and rollout approval. This is not evidence that Leanstral’s base weights are fine-tuned
by the adaptive autoencoder. The concrete contracts and return path are given in Appendix O.
6     How different IRs are used together
6.1   Semantics are indexed by a profile
Each logical view has a signature, sentence language, semantic models, satisfaction relation, and a
supported query fragment. The common record layer does not force one implementation of these
components. A computable representation is not a universal decision procedure: queries may require
decidable fragments, bounded search, or explicit unknown/timeout outcomes. First-order and frame
views express objects and relations; event-calculus views express events, fluents, and change [6];
deontic views express normative force; temporal views bind trace/clock semantics; cognitive views
distinguish agent-indexed knowledge, belief, and intention. World, agent, time, action, and formula
categories cannot be exchanged merely because their identifiers are strings.
For illustration, a normal modality can be interpreted with an indexed accessibility relation:
Different Ri and frame axioms express different profiles. A reflexive epistemic relation supports
factivity; a serial belief relation need not. A deontic ideal-world relation need not make the obligation
true in the actual world. This is an illustrative semantic recipe, not a claim that every repository
view is already compiled by Equation 6. Conditional norms, priorities, defeasible exceptions, and
contrary-to-duty obligations require their own explicit semantics; ordinary normal modal logic is not
a universal deontic solution. LogiKEy provides established semantic embeddings of deontic logics
and combinations in HOL [3].
The repository’s principal view families. TDFOL explicitly combines first-order, temporal, and
deontic syntax; DCEC adds agent-indexed cognitive operators and event-oriented structure. Their
source modules expose these constructors, but constructor availability is distinct from complete
backend coverage. [artifact S20–S21] The same interpreted norm may yield a deontic force/scope
view, frame-based roles, temporal constraints, event/fluent relations, graph traversal edges, and a
supported prover encoding. These are complementary task views. A predicted view distribution
estimates which interfaces deserve attention; it is not a mixture of truth values. The shared symbol
and provenance records permit joins, while each view retains its own semantic profile. [artifact
Bare operator letters are unsafe identifiers: F can mean prohibition or eventually, and G can denote a
cognitive goal or a temporal always operator. Family, profile, operator kind, arguments, and nesting
must survive serialization. In particular, O(Gp) and G(Op) are not equated without a profile-specific
commutation result.
6.2   Loss-aware translation
A translation record must state the source/target views, profile, signature map, assumptions, supported
constructs, named losses, preserved property, and checker evidence. Preserving satisfiability is
different from preserving the truth of an arbitrary query; one-way abstraction is different from
equivalence. Translation validation examines the produced transformation rather than trusting every
invocation of a compiler [7].
A concrete legacy path makes the need visible: the inspected TDFOL-to-FOL converter removes
unary temporal and deontic operators and replaces a binary temporal formula by conjunction. This
may serve as a lossy projection, but it cannot generally carry a modal theorem. The paper does not
attribute this behavior to every adapter. For example, with p false in the actual world and true in every
ideal world, O(p) holds while p does not. On the trace p = [true, false], p holds now but Gp does
not. For strong until, q true now makes p U q true regardless of p now, contradicting the proposed
replacement p ∧ q. [artifact S18]
Encoding a proposition as a predicate such as obligatory(p) also does not supply its semantics. The
representation must distinguish quotation/reification from applying a predicate to a term; relational or
higher-order embeddings must interpret the modality, not simply preserve its spelling.
6.3   A conditional proof-transfer rule
Let Γ |=Ls ϕ be the desired source-view consequence. A translator τ maps the premises and goal
into Lt . Under bridge assumptions B, let RB (s, t) relate admitted source and target models. The
required directionality is:
For every admitted source model satisfying Γ and B, there must be a related target model; otherwise
the relation can be vacuous. If the target checker soundly establishes τ (Γ) |= τ (ϕ), these conditions
transfer the consequence back. A proof sketch appears in Appendix B. This is a contract to discharge
per supported translation, not a soundness theorem about every current extractor.
Cross-source composition introduces further obligations: entity identities must align; timestamps
and units must agree; domain assumptions and exception priorities must be compatible; and the joint
premise set must be consistent in the relevant sense. Under classical logic, inconsistent premises
entail any conclusion. A system that silently adds an assumption to close a proof has changed the
problem rather than solved it.
7   Worked example: learned guidance and cross-view reasoning
Consider a synthetic coding requirement: “Protected resources must not be written without approval.
Each write must be audited within two steps.” It is a specification example, not legal advice or a
production experiment. One source supplies the requirement, a second supplies implementation text,
and a third supplies observations. Let a be an actor, r a resource, and t a discrete trace position.
The normative view may represent the first sentence as:
The policy-to-compliance bridge defines which observed behaviors count as violations. It does not
derive actual non-writing from the obligation. The compliance queries are:
A deterministic implementation model sets Write = ¬ Protected ∨ Approved. Substitution estab-
lishes Equation 10 in that model. An implementation that always writes supplies a counterexample
when the resource is protected and approval is false. Transferring either result to actual source code
requires a justified extraction or refinement relation; finding the word “approve” in a function name is
insufficient.
For Equation 11, an observed write at step 0 and a matching audit at step 1 satisfy the bounded
requirement for that event. A matching audit at step 3 violates the two-step requirement only when the
capture is complete through the relevant deadline and no earlier matching audit exists. An incomplete
window yields unknown, not compliance and not proven violation. The same-looking name in a
different tenant or request cannot be joined without an admitted identity mapping. A global program
guarantee additionally requires reasoning over all modeled executions, not one successful log.
The shared space reuses typed actor/resource/event identities, source maps, and explicit bridge
assumptions. A Legal declaration can state the constraint, an Intent declaration can describe the
proposed workflow, and a Security declaration can supply implementation properties. The intent
is not an observed execution: explicit identity, action, time, and refinement mappings join these
views. The resulting behavioral theorem, trace observation, and policy-applicability decision remain
different conclusions. [artifact S01,S09]
During training, paired variants of this example can change “must” to “may”, move the exception,
or change the audit window. The compiler and view metrics provide candidate targets; independent
annotations determine whether the intended change survived. A family/view head may identify a
temporal omission, a decompiler-plan feature may localize the missing phrase, and a proof-feedback
head may rank a useful obligation. None substitutes for the actual current-profile check. This
example illustrates how the representations cooperate; it is not reported as an executed learned-model
experiment.
8   Evidence and evaluation plan
This revision audits source code at one frozen repository snapshot. It does not execute the full
repository, train a new checkpoint, establish a live CUDA speedup, or show that every supported
head is enabled in the selected deployment. Existing CUDA tests check real gradient work, CPU
parity, clipping, and resident parameters, but they are skipped without suitable hardware and use

9     Related work, limitations, and conclusion
Mathematical autoformalization [1, 2, 9] motivates learned statement generation, but our source
pipeline combines domain-specific parsing, structured targets, adaptive representation heads, and
checked compilation guidance. Learned perception plus symbolic execution is established in neural-
symbolic reasoning [8]; here provenance, modal scope, and separate proof-feedback objectives are
material. We do not claim to originate multi-logic interoperability: institutions formalize signatures,
models, and satisfaction [4], while LogiKEy combines normative logics by HOL embedding [3].
Frame logic, event calculus, and hammer reconstruction are established foundations [5, 6, 10].
The main limitations are teacher bias, possible sample-memory shortcuts, repeated validation-set
selection, unmeasured checkpoint activation, dynamic source behavior, lossy legacy translations,
and bounded backend coverage. The proof space is neither a universal latent space nor a universal
decision procedure. A trained view classifier, valid source map, or high reconstruction score does not
by itself establish faithful interpretation. Result kinds remain distinct: theorem proof, satisfiability,
finite runtime observation, evidence readiness, and policy approval. [artifact S19]
The methodology is best understood as a coupled learning and compilation system: symbolic structure
supplies auditable targets; trainable shared representations expose systematic errors; constrained
proposals and fixed-canary admission improve the compiler-facing path; and modality-aware views
support explicitly justified reasoning. The next result to establish is whether this cycle improves
independent source fidelity and useful cross-view proof coverage on genuinely unseen material, at a
favorable total cost.

B     Preservation contract and proof-transfer argument

F     Source-grounded query procedure
This is a composed method specification, not a claim that one existing function already performs
every step.
1. Bind a query to its source references, target property, ontology, allowed assumptions, and
acceptance profile.
2. Extract and normalize candidate declarations; retain unresolved observations and possible
interpretations.
3. Elaborate each formula against its signature; preserve modality, scope, time, exception, and
source lineage.
4. Resolve cross-source actors, events, resources, and units through admitted bridge records.
5. Select only a target view that supports the required constructs. Unsupported loss causes
abstention or explicit partial analysis.
6. Check compatibility and nonvacuity of the selected premises; create property-preservation
obligations for every relied-upon translation.
7. Invoke an available solver or prover under exact theory, environment, and resource bounds.
Keep candidate, satisfiability, monitor, and kernel-checked outcomes distinct.
8. Reconstruct/check evidence at the assurance level required for the query. Bind the actual
verified statement to the outer artifact fields.
9. Return the conclusion with all assumptions, sources, bridge records, limitations, and result
kind. Unknown does not become true or false by default.
10. On counterexamples, distinguish a bad source interpretation, an inadequate abstraction, an
invalid translation, and a real behavior violation before requesting a repair.

H    Learning-system anatomy and terminology
The original methods draft emphasized generic learned advice. This revision examines the concrete

A useful classification. The concrete adaptive component is a feature-based, multi-head recon-
struction/classification learner with sparse state and a packed tensor execution path. It should not
be described as a variational autoencoder, generative adversarial network, Transformer sequence-
to-sequence formalizer, or trained universal semantic bottleneck without identifying a separate

classification applies to the exact paths audited here.
The three feedback loops. The representation loop changes shared weights. The program-

J.2   The outer model-selection step
The generalizable trainer evaluates family, reconstructed-embedding, global-view, detailed-view,
and combined update candidates. It tries learning-rate multipliers, may select hard examples, can
cap target construction and pre-screen candidates, and compares candidate objective changes with
per-metric regression limits. It temporarily applies candidate state, evaluates, and rolls it back before
deciding which candidate to commit. The evaluated objective also includes view/structural losses,
which need not be differentiable tensors.
This is an inner numerical update surrounded by guarded discrete selection. Calling every stage
backpropagation would be wrong. Equally, describing the tensor path as only heuristic tweaking
would miss its actual backward and parameter-update operations. If validation samples are absent,
evaluation falls back to training examples; that case must not be labeled held-out validation. A
nonzero deadband changes the acceptance policy and must be disclosed, not buried as a numerical
implementation detail.
J.3   Proof-feedback heads and objective isolation
The categorical heads are obligation family, trusted outcome, and reconstruction success. The
multilabel heads are semantic slots, premise family, proof-route availability, and minimal failing
contract. The default vocabulary and family-context sizes are bounded. A head can abstain when its
confidence or available labels are inadequate.
Training accepts only records passing trust, partition, and compiler/toolchain version checks. Dupli-
cate IDs are not trained repeatedly. The first admissible version may pin previously empty proof-head
state; mismatches are excluded. The implementation compares protected objective fingerprints and
reports a proof-loss weight of zero in the primary representation objective. This is a useful causal
design: proof feedback can teach prediction and route selection without being permitted to rewrite
the statement solely to maximize provability. Actual downstream benefit still needs an ablation.

K.1   Grammar controls the candidate language
The decoder implementation declares typed productions and a frozen vocabulary of 143 tokens,

categories. Its declared masks are valid token, grammar, binder, type and family; its search bounds
are 16 beam entries and 64 decode steps. These are implementation constants, not results of a newly
trained model. The exact profile and any changes belong in the run manifest.
This provides an engineered output language in which a model may rank candidates. It prevents
impossible JSON shapes or invalid family/type combinations from receiving metric credit. It does
not guarantee correct grounding, truth, faithful negation or exception scope. A fallback involving an
admitted reference or gold artifact is not an independent blind prediction and must be excluded or

K.2    Feature export is not source copying
The stable learned export restricts outputs to reusable feature groups such as compiler contracts,

The product is a content-addressed guidance record: target contract and family, bounded features,

Introspection compares predicted and target families/views, decoded and target embeddings, semantic-

caused by poor shared family ranking can lead to a parameter update; loss caused by an unhandled

N.2   Vector indexing is separate from representation learning
The FAISS store maintains numerical indexes, per-collection metadata, and mappings between

interpreted, and a store over vectors does not establish that those vectors came from this autoencoder.

dispatch does not execute a vector query. Actual vector search must therefore be attributed to another

N.3   Graphs connect evidence without silently adding axioms
The thin client can retrieve incoming/outgoing adjacency records and execute bounded walks over
CID-linked nodes. Its results retain neighbor identifiers and edge metadata. A graph can connect
a source passage to a definition, entity, related artifact, or dependency; an index edge does not
necessarily assert a logical implication. [artifact S34]
At the query boundary, lexical and vector hits can nominate seeds, graph navigation can expand their
context, and exact artifact identities can retrieve declarations. This is a proposed composition of the
available interfaces, not a measured fusion algorithm. A premise-admission stage must then inspect
source lineage, entity and temporal alignment, domain applicability, declared authority, and the
relevant interpretation. Keep “retrieved”, “admitted premise”, “assumed”, and “proved” as separate
states.
Identity and reuse. The inward IR kernel binds canonicalization profile, domain, schema, collection
semantics, and payload into content identity. A CID identifies those bytes; it is not a proof of meaning.
Reuse of a proof or translation must also bind the relevant premises, theory, toolchain, policy, and
checker evidence. Similarity retrieval is not an exact-result cache, and equality of an embedding is
not equality of canonical declarations. [artifact S01]
O     Tactician, Hammer, and Leanstral: distinct computational roles
O.1   Planning is deterministic until explicitly guided
The local LogicTactician validates the goal and policy, binds the configuration identity, validates
and partitions candidate sources, optionally applies pinned guidance, selects routes under budgets, and
decomposes declared proof gaps. Cycles cause abstention rather than a malformed plan. Excluded
sources retain a reason, and final plans carry input roots and guidance identities. The planner’s own
implementation performs no proof, write, or network work. [artifact S38]
This is a domain-neutral orchestration layer. Its name should not be taken to imply implementation of
an external tactic-learning system. A separate executor is needed to realize a plan, and that execution
must supply its own artifacts and outcomes. Optional ranking and nomination have a narrower
contract than unconstrained generation of new assumptions or arbitrary executable tasks.
O.2   The supported-fragment Hammer workflow
The inspected Hammer guide describes a native goal, premise selection, translation to TPTP or SMT-
LIB, a bounded external portfolio, candidate normalization, reconstruction, kernel checking, and
receipt persistence. Each target ITP has a frontend and matching reconstructor. The first-order-safe
fragment admits explicit term/connective forms and finite sort signatures under the translation contract;
unsupported dependent types, higher-order predicate quantification, unresolved polymorphism, and
opaque unrecognized terms must return unsupported rather than be erased. [artifact S37]
All external solvers require operator opt-in. A missing native toolchain remains unavailable; a timeout
remains a timeout. In this ITP Hammer contract, a solver’s answer is an untrusted candidate until the
originating native checker accepts reconstruction. This statement is specific to that contract; another
SMT-facing API may report a solver-local result without representing it as a native ITP theorem.
[artifact S19,S37]
A theorem applies to the formalized premises and goal. It does not independently establish that the
original prose, source-code extractor, or cross-domain identity mapping was correct. In particular,
a valid reconstructed proof of an incorrectly simplified obligation does not repair the semantic loss
caused by the simplification.
O.3    What the optional premise selector actually learns
The deterministic baseline uses symbol, type, import, and graph-overlap features. The optional
selector artifact applies a bounded linear score followed by a sigmoid, with additional count features
and a pinned model digest. The supplied default weights are hand-authored. Its documentation
explicitly does not claim a trained neural or tree-based checkpoint. A genuinely learned artifact can
fit the same interface, but the training dataset, loss, split, parameter provenance, and evaluation would
then require separate evidence. [artifact S36]
The documented held-out benchmark uses shared-import proximity as a relevance proxy because
the fixture corpus lacks explicit theorem-to-theorem dependency labels. Recall or reciprocal rank
against that proxy is not ground-truth proof-premise recall. A digest binds the loaded artifact; it
neither demonstrates training nor proves that the source of the digest was independently trusted.
O.4    Leanstral does not train itself by generating a draft
The security proof-assistant lane treats Leanstral output as advisory and checks the proposed Lean
code against a designated proof consumer. Its policy rejects proof bypasses such as sorry, admit,
or unapproved axioms. Configuration readiness, an actual model call, a generated candidate, and a
checker-accepted proof are different events. The source audit does not demonstrate fine-tuning of
Leanstral’s base weights. [artifact S39]
The legal rollout gives the return path to learning an explicit artifact boundary. Candidate JSON or
free-form drafts are audit inputs only. Structured guidance that passes the required syntax, provenance,
anti-copy, proof, and configured reconstruction checks may enter the trusted feature bus and bounded
autoencoder training. A stable source-free export remains inert until its independent promotion gate
accepts it. A deterministic compiler/decompiler patch is a separately versioned executable change
with focused tests and frozen-canary evidence. [artifact S40]
The documented rollout is an ordered smoke, hyperparameter-selection, fixed-canary, and production
sequence. Promotion checks per-family semantics, reconstruction, source-copy behavior, trusted-
feedback receipt agreement, process outcomes, queue telemetry, accepted-patch rate, and rollback
identity. These are documented control requirements, not evidence that this manuscript executed or
completed such a rollout.
P     Putting the representations and update loops together
This explanatory procedure composes inspected interfaces while explicitly separating design from
execution. It is not a claim that one repository function implements the entire procedure with every
optional component enabled.
Construct and ground. Begin with a versioned source and provenance. Retrieve candidate frames
or context through the configured lexical, numerical, or graph route. Compile an interpretation using
the chosen domain adapter and record ambiguity or unsupported semantics. Preserve the canonical
declaration independently of any learned feature vector. Numerical targets identify their producer;
compiler-derived targets identify their teacher. [artifact S01,S07,S22,S34,S35]
Project and challenge. Produce named logical views using shared symbols and explicit projection
contracts. A frame view records roles, a deontic view records normative force, a temporal view
records clock relations, and an event view records transitions. Source-withheld decompilation exposes
missing reconstructable information. Minimal pairs and independent annotations challenge omissions
that a compiler/decompiler cycle could share. [artifact S04,S07,S09,S31]
Plan, propose, and check. A query generates obligations under the relevant interpretation. The
Tactician selects bounded routes from admitted candidates. A Hammer can search a supported
translation and attempt native reconstruction; Leanstral may instead suggest or repair a candidate in an
approved lane. Record failure, counterexample, timeout, unsupported translation, and unavailability
distinctly. Only the actual checker and its pinned inputs establish the scope of a checked result.
[artifact S37–S39]
Improve the right component. An embedding residual or family/view classification defect can
motivate a shared-parameter update. A repeated loss of exception scope can motivate a com-
piler/decompiler code change. A poorly selected proof route can motivate an isolated proof-head
update, using only admitted eligible feedback. These diagnoses are examples of how to use the avail-
able signals, not measured examples of autonomous learning. Teacher fidelity, primary representation
quality, proof-head calibration, and executable repair correctness remain different objectives. [artifact
Promote and reuse. Freeze the accepted model or executable change, its targets, data split, con-
figuration, and evidence. Source-free guidance requires independent fixed-canary promotion and a
receipt that the evaluated consumer actually loaded it. Reuse exact artifacts with their dependency
identities, not merely similar vectors. Keep untouched test data separate from model-selection and
canary populations. [artifact S01,S24,S30,S40]
P.1   Legal, Intent, and Security IR composition
For the main paper’s protected-write example, a Legal declaration can express an applicable constraint,
an Intent declaration can describe a plan to request approval and write, and a Security declaration
can model whether the implementation enforces the check. An event/trace view can then describe
observed requests and writes. A shared name is not sufficient to join them: actor, resource, tenant,
operation, time, and policy-version mappings must be admitted. [artifact S01,S04,S09]
The plan’s postcondition is not evidence that it occurred. A permission in an intent or policy view is
not a record of execution. A proof that a model enforces a guard is not a legal-applicability decision.
The useful common space is therefore a collection of linked typed declarations and evidence records,
with explicit bridge obligations, rather than one blended verdict or universal latent representation.
A learned view head can recommend examining temporal structure, but the temporal bridge must
still specify its clock and scope. A graph can locate a candidate exemption provision, but the source
interpretation must establish applicability. A counterexample can reveal a model defect, but a changed
compiler must not remove the difficult premise merely to make the theorem provable. These are the
practical reasons for keeping retrieval, semantic interpretation, statistical guidance, and checking
separate while permitting structured feedback among them.
Q    Additional retrieval and proof-assistance evaluation
The training arms T0–T5 remain unchanged. Retrieval and proof-assistance conditions should be
evaluated on the same frozen tasks, with controlled budgets, rather than folded into an unexplained
end-to-end score. The following are proposed experiments; no outcomes are claimed in this revision.
For all conditions, retain the corpus and index revision, tokenizer, embedding producer, index
implementation, model digest, admitted premises, goal root, logical profile, supported translation
fragment, toolchain, checker, time/memory limits, and outcome. Record fixture or mock targets
explicitly. Count unsupported, unavailable, and abstained cases in coverage denominators rather than
reporting only successful requests. End-to-end cost includes target construction, indexing, gradient
updates, model calls, failed candidates, proof reconstruction, semantic validation, and human review.
These experiments distinguish three hypotheses: better access to relevant context; better search under
a fixed formal interpretation; and better fidelity of that interpretation to the source. Improvements in
one do not establish improvements in the other two. No new performance value, trained checkpoint,
native solver execution, or deployment qualification is inferred from rebuilding this paper.
Paper checklist: official questionnaire required
The uploaded workshop research template includes checklist.tex, but that questionnaire was not
included in the supplied sources. This page is a compilation placeholder, not an official questionnaire
and not a set of completed compliance answers.
